title: Enterprise and organisation

blocks.heading: Enterprise and organisation
blocks.text: Enterprise is organising productive resources and undertaking the decisions and risks involved in production. Organisation of production concerns who makes productive decisions and how resources are coordinated; land ownership concerns rights over one resource. A group with land, workers and equipment still needs decisions about what to make, how to obtain inputs and who will buy the output. Individual producers, cooperatives, companies and state organisations can undertake these tasks. Their strengths and limitations depend on finance, accountability, scale and aims; the label alone does not establish efficiency.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Individual production
blocks.text: Individual production is production organised by an individual producer rather than jointly by a membership or state organisation. Individual control can allow direct decisions but may limit the finance, time or skills available to organise larger activities. An invented self-employed repairer decides which jobs to accept and obtains the needed tools. Individual organisation does not mean the person owns every resource used: a workshop or land may be rented. Distinguish productive organisation from rights over the premises.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Cooperatives
blocks.text: A cooperative is an organisation owned and operated jointly by members to meet shared economic or social needs. Pooling resources can give members access to equipment or services they could not obtain individually, while decisions and benefits require workable member arrangements. Small growers might jointly organise storage and sales. Members must agree contributions, responsibilities and how decisions are made. Common purpose does not remove coordination problems. A cooperative can operate on rented land, so it is not itself a land-ownership category.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Companies
blocks.text: A company is an incorporated organisation with a legal identity separate from its owners, through which production or other activities can be organised. Ownership and management can be separated, allowing resources and decisions to be organised beyond one individual, though coordination and accountability remain necessary. Understand the productive arrangement here rather than detailed company law. A company can be locally owned, state-owned or part of a wider international group. Company status alone does not show what land it owns or whether its production benefits all local people.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Transnational or multinational companies
blocks.text: A transnational or multinational company is a company that operates productive activities across more than one country. Cross-border organisation can connect finance, technology and markets, but local development gains depend on employment, local links and the retention of benefits. An invented processing group operating facilities in two countries illustrates the definition. Selling an occasional export alone does not establish that a business operates production in several countries. Compare actual operations. Potential investment benefits do not guarantee fair work, local purchasing or low environmental harm.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: State organisations
blocks.text: State organisations are bodies through which the state owns or organises productive activities or services. They may pursue access and public-service goals as well as financial objectives, but need resources, management and accountability to deliver them. A fictional state-owned water provider illustrates productive service organisation. State ownership is different from communal control by a local membership. A service goal does not prove effective delivery: maintenance, staffing and access evidence still matter.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Organisation differs from resource ownership
blocks.text: Four invented growers each own separate plots but jointly own and manage a cooperative to buy inputs and sell crops. Private plot ownership describes their land rights; cooperative organisation describes how part of production is coordinated. The categories are compatible, not competing answers to one question. A group seeking shared equipment access might use a cooperative if members can agree contributions and responsibilities. Individual production gives direct control but may offer fewer pooled resources; a company or state organisation has different arrangements to assess.
